text: Knowing when an LLM is wrong: uncertainty estimation methods, and the LM-Polygraph library
Ahmad Bin Qasim
Problem:Confidently wrong
High-confidence errors
A wrong answer can carry near-certain probability.

Four BioASQ answers from the 7B model. Each is incorrect against the reference, and each was assigned a probability above 0.98 by the model itself. The text of an answer gives no indication of which to verify.
Selective answering
Withholding the least certain answers raises the accuracy of the rest.

Accuracy of the answers that remain as the most uncertain are progressively withheld, ranked by mean token entropy. Withholding half raises the accuracy of the remainder from 45% to 67%. An uninformative score follows the flat line; a perfect ranking follows the upper dashed line. AUROC, reported throughout, measures how far a ranking separates correct answers from incorrect ones.
Methods: Wherethe uncertainty is
Where the signal comes from
Two properties locate every estimator: the model access it needs and the number of answers it draws.

Position further right indicates greater access required: a hosted API exposes text only, an open model also exposes token probabilities and hidden states. The lower row samples the same question several times. The next slide places every estimator in these families; the three after it each open up one method on the same two answers, and the fourth covers trained probes.
Every estimator, by type and tier
Type denotes the signal an estimator reads; tier, what it requires to run.

The twenty estimators compared in this talk, placed by signal type and tier. Tiers are cumulative: T1 needs no sampling (the answering pass, plus a question-free pass for the two PMIs), T2 adds a second prompt, T3 adds sampling, and T4 adds a DeBERTa NLI model over the samples. Consistency and sampling methods divide between T3 and T4 according to whether they require the NLI model. The later slides use these tiers to group the results.
Information-based: mean token entropy
A model unsure of the next token spreads its probability; mean token entropy averages that spread over the answer.

Two answers from Qwen2.5-3B. Each chip is one generated token, with the entropy of the distribution it was chosen from. The right answer was near-certain at every step; the wrong one was a guess from its first token. Of the 20 estimators, mean token entropy ranked first on both Qwen models.
Self-report: p(True)
Shown its own answer, the model is asked whether it is true; the score is the probability it puts on “True”.

The same two answers, put back to the model in a second prompt. Here p(True) separates them cleanly, yet over the 1,000 questions it ranked 16th of 20 on the 3B model and was at chance on the 7B. For the right answer “(A” took 15% of the probability, which a score reading only “True” ignores.
Sampling-based: lexical similarity
Ask the same question again: answers that change from sample to sample signal uncertainty.

Ten answers sampled at temperature 1 for each question, compared pair by pair by ROUGE-L word overlap. For the right answer all ten agree; for the wrong one they scatter, and four of them name the reference answer the greedy answer missed. Sampling makes it tier 3; it reads only text, so it works with any API.
Trained probes
A classifier on the model's hidden states can predict incorrectness, given labelled data.
Probes require graded answers from the task they will be applied to, and retraining for each new task or model. They are included here for completeness and were not run.
Tooling: LM-Polygraph
LM-Polygraph
One library implements most of these estimators behind one interface.

Open source and pip-installable. An estimator returns one uncertainty score per answer, higher indicating less certainty; grading the answers and scoring the estimators against those grades are separate steps.
The method catalogue
Thirty-eight methods in five categories, with the infrastructure to compare them.

Categories and counts are LM-Polygraph's own, taken from its README; the grey note on each bar gives the nearest family from the methods slides. Density-based and ensembling methods require training data or several models, and were not run here.
Tooling:Your model, your data
Wrapping a model
One wrapper, for a local model or an API.

WhiteboxModel takes a Hugging Face model and tokenizer; BlackboxModel takes an API, which restricts the available estimators to black-box methods unless log-probabilities are returned. Eager attention is required on transformers 5.x. The left-hand block was executed as shown; its output appears beneath it.
UEManager: dataset-level evaluation
One object runs every estimator over a dataset and scores each ranking.

Each answer receives a quality score from the generation metric and an uncertainty score from every estimator; the UE metric then measures how closely each estimator's ranking follows the quality. The BioASQ study is this call with 20 estimators and a task-specific grader.
Defining a new estimator
A new method is a class with three members, and it works with everything on the previous slides.
This estimator scores an answer by its least likely token. It was run inside UEManager alongside the built-in estimators, sharing their statistics.
Example:A small BioASQ study
The evaluation set: BioASQ factoids
1,000 biomedical factoid questions, each with a short reference answer.

Questions are drawn from the BioASQ challenges and retained only where the reference answer is at most five words, so correctness can be determined. Answers are graded by exact match, then by token rules, then by manual labels where no rule applies. The labels were proposed with LLM assistance and reviewed; they were not set by domain experts.
Every estimator, ranked
Tier 1 contains both the strongest estimator and the weakest.

AUROC for separating wrong answers from correct ones, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Dark blue marks tier 1: no sampling and no second model. Hollow markers are sign-inverted, returning a confidence rather than an uncertainty, and are read as 1−AUROC.
What each tier adds
Sampling and an NLI model narrow the spread without raising the maximum.

Each dot is one estimator, placed in its tier; the bar marks the tier median. Tiers are cumulative: each column adds one requirement to the preceding one — a second prompt, then sampling, then a DeBERTa NLI model over the samples.
Conclusions and outlook
Scope and limitations
An introduction rather than a benchmark: the ranking is specific to this setting.
The ranking is conditioned on one dataset, one prompt and one grading procedure. Replicating the comparison on a target task and model is a short script in LM-Polygraph.
Summary
The families differ in the access they need; the ranking between them is task-specific.
Point three is the only item drawn from the BioASQ results, and the preceding slide gives its range across models. The remainder is independent of the task.
References
Sources for the methods, the library and the data.
The key on the left indicates what each paper supports, in the colour used for it on the method slides. The LM-Polygraph README cites a paper for each of its 38 methods.
Backup
The scores behind the AUROC
The tier-1 and tier-4 score distributions overlap to a similar degree.

Raw uncertainty scores for every question, separated by whether the answer was graded correct. An AUROC near 0.8 still corresponds to substantially overlapping distributions: the score supports triage, not a decision on an individual answer. Semantic entropy as lm-polygraph computes it can fall below zero; only the ordering of scores matters.
The same methods on six models
Among single-pass estimators, only mean token entropy transfers.

Each line traces one estimator's AUROC across six instruction-tuned models from four families; a flat line indicates stability. Mean pairwise Spearman ρ = 0.87, so the ranking is largely preserved. Mean token entropy is the only tier-1 estimator above 0.75 on every model (0.76–0.83); maximum sequence probability and perplexity, computed from the same forward pass, fall to approximately 0.60 on Mistral. The best tier-4 estimator exceeds mean token entropy by a significant margin on two of the six (paired bootstrap). All runs use the same 1,000 questions and the full manual label set.
